Proverbs 1.audience: Proverbs is addressed as a father's instruction to "my son" (Proverbs 1:8). Its first readers were young men learning how to live wisely in Israelite society.

culture.title: Wisdom teaching in the ancient world
culture.text: Egypt and Mesopotamia had collections of wise sayings, often written as a father's or official's advice to a son, such as the Egyptian Instruction of Ptahhotep.

culture.title: Wisdom crying in the streets
culture.text: Wisdom is pictured as a woman calling out at the city gates and in the busy squares—where public life took place.

culture.title: Ornaments of grace
culture.text: A father's teaching is "an ornament of grace unto thy head, and chains about thy neck"—like jewelry worn with pride.

Proverbs 2.audience: The father urges his son to seek wisdom like hidden treasure and warns him against "the strange woman" (Proverbs 2:16).

culture.title: Searching for hidden treasures
culture.text: In times of war, people buried silver and valuables. Finding such a hoard was a stroke of fortune (Matthew 13:44).

culture.title: The covenant of her God
culture.text: The adulteress has forgotten "the covenant of her God"—marriage was seen as a covenant made before God (Malachi 2:14).

Proverbs 3.audience: Proverbs 3 is quoted in the New Testament: verses 11–12 in Hebrews 12:5–6 and verse 34 in James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5.

culture.title: Firstfruits and full barns
culture.text: Honoring the LORD with the firstfruits of the harvest was commanded in the law (Exodus 23:19). Full barns and overflowing winepresses were signs of a good year.

culture.title: Binding on the neck
culture.text: "Bind them about thy neck; write them upon the table of thine heart"—like a necklace or a writing tablet.

culture.title: Withholding wages
culture.text: Telling a neighbor to come back tomorrow when you have what is owed was condemned; day laborers needed their pay each day.

Proverbs 4.audience: The father recalls being taught by his own father (Proverbs 4:3–4). Wisdom was passed from generation to generation in the home.

culture.title: Two paths
culture.text: The path of the just grows brighter like dawn; the way of the wicked is like darkness where people stumble without seeing why.

culture.title: A crown of glory
culture.text: Wisdom gives "a crown of glory"—garlands and crowns were worn at feasts and celebrations.

Proverbs 5.audience: The father warns his son against adultery and urges faithfulness to "the wife of thy youth" (Proverbs 5:18).

culture.title: Drinking from your own cistern
culture.text: Every household depended on its own cistern or well for water. The image describes faithfulness within one's own marriage.

culture.title: Lips that drop honey
culture.text: "The lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb"—sweet speech that hides danger.

Proverbs 6.audience: This chapter covers several matters of daily life: standing surety for debts, laziness, troublemakers, and adultery.

culture.title: Striking hands as surety
culture.text: Striking hands with a stranger was a pledge to pay his debt if he did not. Proverbs repeatedly warns against it (Proverbs 11:15; 22:26).

culture.title: The ant
culture.text: Harvester ants in the land gather and store seeds in summer for the winter.

culture.title: Seven things God hates
culture.text: "Six things... yea, seven" is a number pattern common in Hebrew and ancient Near Eastern wisdom sayings (also Proverbs 30:15–31).

Proverbs 7.audience: Readers who already knew the father's earlier warnings about the adulterous woman (chapters 2, 5, and 6) would recognize this scene as that same danger acted out in vivid, memorable detail rather than as a report of one identified incident.

culture.title: Looking through the casement
culture.text: Windows had lattices (casements) that let people look out without being seen.

culture.title: Peace offerings paid
culture.text: "I have peace offerings with me; this day have I payed my vows." Meat from a peace offering had to be eaten quickly, and she invites him to share the feast.

culture.title: Egyptian linen and spices
culture.text: Her bed has fine linen of Egypt and is perfumed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon—costly imported luxuries.

Proverbs 8.audience: Later readers, Jewish and Christian alike, treasured this chapter for how it ties everyday wisdom to creation itself; many Christian readers have also heard an echo of Christ in Wisdom's nearness to God before the world began.

culture.title: Calling at the gates
culture.text: City gates were where business, law, and public announcements took place.

culture.title: Better than rubies
culture.text: Precious stones, silver, and fine gold were the highest measures of wealth.

culture.title: Setting a compass on the deep
culture.text: "When he set a compass upon the face of the depth"—a circle or boundary marked out, like a builder drawing a line.

Proverbs 9.audience: Wisdom and Folly, both pictured as women, invite passers-by to their houses. Readers would choose between their two feasts.

culture.title: Seven pillars
culture.text: Wisdom's house has seven pillars—a large, well-built house. Pillared houses are known from Israelite towns.

culture.title: Mixed wine
culture.text: Wine was often mixed with water or spices before serving at a banquet.

culture.title: Stolen waters
culture.text: "Stolen waters are sweet"—water taken from another's cistern, a picture of forbidden pleasure.

Proverbs 10.audience: Readers moving from the sustained father-to-son appeal of chapters 1–9 would notice the different literary form here: brief, two-line observations meant to be weighed one at a time rather than followed as a single continuous argument.

culture.title: Two-line sayings
culture.text: Most of these proverbs have two lines that contrast with each other—"A wise son maketh a glad father: but a foolish son is the heaviness of his mother."

culture.title: Gathering in summer
culture.text: Harvest work had to be done in its season. A son who sleeps at harvest brings shame.

Proverbs 11.audience: These sayings deal with honesty in business, generosity, and the effect of the righteous and wicked on a city (Proverbs 11:10–11).

culture.title: False balances
culture.text: Merchants weighed goods with stone weights on balance scales. Dishonest traders used false weights; many stone weights have been found in Israel.

culture.title: Withholding grain
culture.text: Hoarding grain to raise prices in a shortage brought the people's curse; selling it brought blessing.

culture.title: A jewel in a swine's snout
culture.text: Women wore nose rings. A gold ring in a pig's snout pictures beauty without discretion.

Proverbs 12.audience: These sayings cover family, work, speech, and honesty—the everyday matters of a farming household.

culture.title: A virtuous wife as a crown
culture.text: "A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband"—a wife's character affected the whole family's honor.

culture.title: Caring for animals
culture.text: "A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast"—the law required care for working animals (Deuteronomy 25:4).

culture.title: Tilling the land
culture.text: Most Israelites were farmers. Working one's own land brought bread; chasing worthless schemes brought poverty.

Proverbs 13.audience: These sayings address speech, wealth, discipline of children, and the value of good company.

culture.title: The rod of discipline
culture.text: Physical discipline of children was standard in the ancient world. Proverbs connects it with a parent's love.

culture.title: An inheritance for grandchildren
culture.text: Land and property passed from generation to generation within the family.

Proverbs 14.audience: These sayings contrast the wise and the foolish in home, work, and community, including how the poor are treated (Proverbs 14:21, 31).

culture.title: Oxen and clean cribs
culture.text: "Where no oxen are, the crib is clean"—an empty manger is tidy, but without oxen there is no plowing and no harvest.

culture.title: A king's people
culture.text: A large population was a king's strength and honor.

Proverbs 15.audience: These sayings stress gentle speech, contentment, and the LORD's watch over all people.

culture.title: A dinner of herbs
culture.text: "Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith." Fattened beef was a rare luxury; vegetables were a poor man's meal.

culture.title: A hedge of thorns
culture.text: Thorny hedges protected fields but made paths impassable. The lazy man's way seems blocked by them.

Proverbs 16.audience: These sayings speak of God's sovereignty over human plans and of the king's responsibility for justice.

culture.title: Casting the lot
culture.text: Lots—marked stones or sticks—were cast into the fold of a garment to make decisions. The whole outcome is "of the LORD."

culture.title: Weights of the bag
culture.text: Merchants carried their stone weights in a bag. Honest weights belong to the LORD.

culture.title: The hoary head
culture.text: Grey hair was honored as a crown of glory, a sign of long life and wisdom.

Proverbs 17.audience: These sayings address family peace, friendship, bribes, and justice in the courts.

culture.title: A dry morsel
culture.text: "Better is a dry morsel, and quietness therewith, than an house full of sacrifices with strife"—a house full of feasting on sacrificial meat.

culture.title: Refining pots
culture.text: Silver was refined in a crucible and gold in a furnace, but the LORD tests hearts.

culture.title: Gifts in secret
culture.text: "A wicked man taketh a gift out of the bosom to pervert the ways of judgment"—a bribe passed from the fold of a garment.

Proverbs 18.audience: These sayings deal with speech, pride, and fairness in hearing both sides of a case (Proverbs 18:17).

culture.title: A strong tower
culture.text: Cities had fortified towers where people could flee in an attack.

culture.title: A gift that makes room
culture.text: A gift could open the way to an audience with the great—a common custom when approaching officials.

Proverbs 19.audience: These sayings discuss the poor, false witnesses, discipline, and the king's anger and favor.

culture.title: Lending to the LORD
culture.text: "He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the LORD."

culture.title: A continual dropping
culture.text: Flat earthen roofs leaked in heavy rain. A quarrelsome wife is compared to constant dripping.

culture.title: Hand in the dish
culture.text: People ate with their hands from a common dish. The lazy man won't even bring his hand back to his mouth.

Proverbs 20.audience: These sayings address wine, the king's justice, honest weights, and rash vows.

culture.title: Plowing in cold weather
culture.text: Plowing was done in the cold, rainy season after the autumn rains. The lazy man skips it and has nothing at harvest.

culture.title: Divers weights
culture.text: "Divers weights, and divers measures"—two sets of weights, one for buying and one for selling, were a common fraud.

culture.title: The lamp going out
culture.text: A lamp kept burning through the night was a sign of a living household. A put-out lamp pictures a family line ended.

Proverbs 21.audience: These sayings stress that God weighs hearts and that justice matters more than sacrifice (Proverbs 21:3).

culture.title: Rivers of water in the king's heart
culture.text: Farmers directed irrigation water through channels. God turns the king's heart as easily.

culture.title: A corner of the housetop
culture.text: Flat roofs were used as living space. Living in a corner of the roof is better than sharing a house with a contentious wife.

culture.title: The horse prepared for battle
culture.text: Horses were used mainly for war chariots. Victory comes from the LORD.

Proverbs 22.audience: From Proverbs 22:17 a new section begins, "the words of the wise." Parts of Proverbs 22:17–24:22 closely resemble the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope.

culture.title: The ancient landmark
culture.text: Boundary stones marked family land. Moving them was theft, condemned in the law and in Egyptian wisdom too (Deuteronomy 19:14).

culture.title: Thirty sayings
culture.text: "Excellent things" may be read ‘thirty sayings’; the Instruction of Amenemope is arranged in thirty chapters.

culture.title: Standing before kings
culture.text: A skilled worker would serve kings, not obscure men—royal courts sought out the best craftsmen and scribes.

Proverbs 23.audience: These sayings advise on eating with rulers, avoiding greed, honoring parents, and the dangers of wine.

culture.title: A knife to the throat
culture.text: Eating at a ruler's table required restraint; the dainties could be "deceitful meat" offered with a hidden purpose.

culture.title: Riches with wings
culture.text: Riches "fly away as an eagle toward heaven." Amenemope has a similar picture of wealth flying away like geese.

culture.title: Wine that moves itself aright
culture.text: The description of drunkenness—redness of eyes, wounds without cause, confusion—is given in close detail, ending with the drunkard seeking yet another drink (Proverbs 23:35).

Proverbs 24.audience: This chapter ends "the words of the wise" and adds further sayings "of the wise" (Proverbs 24:23).

culture.title: The field of the slothful
culture.text: An untended vineyard is overgrown with thorns and nettles, and its stone wall broken down—a familiar sight in the hill country.

culture.title: Building after preparing fields
culture.text: "Prepare thy work without, and make it fit for thyself in the field; and afterwards build thine house"—secure a living before building a home.

Proverbs 25.audience: Readers in and after Hezekiah's reign, a time of religious reform and renewed interest in Judah's written heritage, would have recognized this heading as evidence that older royal wisdom was still being gathered and valued generations after Solomon.

culture.title: Scribes at Hezekiah's court
culture.text: Royal scribes copied and preserved texts. Hezekiah's reign was a time of religious reform and literary activity.

culture.title: Snow in harvest
culture.text: Snow brought down from the mountains could cool drinks for reapers in the summer heat—refreshing like a faithful messenger.

culture.title: Coals of fire on the head
culture.text: Feeding a hungry enemy will "heap coals of fire upon his head." Paul quotes it in Romans 12:20.

Proverbs 26.audience: These sayings describe the fool, the sluggard, the meddler, and the gossip. Peter quotes verse 11 (2 Peter 2:22).

culture.title: Snow in summer, rain in harvest
culture.text: Snow in summer and rain at harvest were unseasonable and damaging—as unfitting as honor for a fool.

culture.title: A whip for the horse
culture.text: "A whip for the horse, a bridle for the ass, and a rod for the fool's back."

culture.title: Taking a dog by the ears
culture.text: Dogs in the ancient Near East were mostly half-wild. Grabbing one by the ears invites a bite.

Proverbs 27.audience: These sayings deal with friendship, boasting, and caring for one's flocks and herds (Proverbs 27:23–27).

culture.title: Iron sharpening iron
culture.text: Iron blades were sharpened against other iron or stone.

culture.title: Knowing the state of your flocks
culture.text: Lambs supplied clothing, goats paid for fields, and goats' milk fed the household—a herder's wealth outlasts riches and crowns.

culture.title: Blessing loudly in the morning
culture.text: Shouting a blessing to a neighbor early in the morning is counted a curse—manners mattered.

Proverbs 28.audience: These sayings contrast the righteous and wicked, especially in rulers and in the treatment of the poor.

culture.title: A sweeping rain
culture.text: A poor man who oppresses the poor is like a heavy rain that washes away the crops instead of watering them.

culture.title: Increasing wealth by usury
culture.text: Charging interest to the poor was forbidden (Leviticus 25:36). Such wealth ends up with someone who will pity the poor.

Proverbs 29.audience: Readers who had followed the sayings on rulers and the poor since chapter 25 would hear this chapter's close as the climax of that theme, tying a ruler's justice and a people's trust in the LORD together one final time.

culture.title: Where there is no vision
culture.text: "Vision" here means prophetic revelation. Without it, "the people perish" (literally, cast off restraint).

culture.title: A king who judges the poor faithfully
culture.text: Ancient kings were expected to defend the poor and the orphan. Hammurabi's law code makes the same claim for its king.

Proverbs 30.audience: Proverbs 30 is "the words of Agur the son of Jakeh" (Proverbs 30:1), otherwise unknown. It includes numerical sayings: "There be three things... yea, four."

culture.title: Numerical sayings
culture.text: Sayings listing three or four things that share something were a common form of ancient wisdom.

culture.title: Small but wise creatures
culture.text: Ants, conies (rock hyraxes), locusts, and spiders (or lizards) are small but show wisdom—storing food, living in rocks, moving in order, and living in kings' palaces.

culture.title: The leech's daughters
culture.text: The horseleach, a blood-sucking leech common in pools, pictures endless craving.

Proverbs 31.audience: Readers familiar with Hebrew acrostic poems, such as several psalms, would recognize the alphabetic structure of verses 10–31 as a deliberate literary form meant to present the capable woman as a complete, well-rounded picture from A to Z.

culture.title: A queen mother's advice
culture.text: Royal mothers had influence at court. Lemuel's mother warns against women and wine and urges him to defend the poor.

culture.title: Distaff and spindle
culture.text: Wool and flax were spun by hand with a spindle and distaff, a constant task for women in the household.

culture.title: Scarlet clothing
culture.text: Her household is clothed in scarlet—dyed wool, warm and costly—so she does not fear the snow.
